messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Taxi/Uber Driver
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 27-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a rideshare driver in a mid-sized American city. He came to the intake session quietly, choosing the seat farthest from the door, and spoke in measured sentences that occasionally broke apart when the material became too close. He has never sought mental health support before. What finally brought him in, he said, was that he had nearly driven his car off an overpass three weeks ago — not by accident.

The abuse began when Kwame was around six and continued until he was fourteen, carried out by his father, a man who worked nights and came home in the early hours smelling of alcohol and something else Kwame still cannot name. The worst episodes followed a particular pattern: Kwame would hear the slow, heavy footsteps on the wooden hallway floor outside his bedroom, and the sound alone was enough to make his body lock. His father favoured the cold — winter mornings, the window left open — and Kwame learned to associate the bite of cold air on his skin with what was about to happen. The beatings often involved a leather belt, and the specific texture of that material — rough, cracked, slightly warm from his father's hand — became encoded into those nights in a way that no amount of time has fully erased.

Kwame left his family home at seventeen and has not returned. He moved through community college, a series of jobs, and eventually into rideshare driving, which suited him because he could control the environment, control who entered and left, and, crucially, drive away. But the cab of his car has not been the sanctuary he imagined. Passengers sometimes wear belts with a particular texture he catches in his peripheral mirror. In winter, cold air floods the car when someone opens the door, and the temperature on his skin — that specific chill — arrives before any conscious thought does, and his body is already somewhere else. When a passenger walks up behind the car or he hears footsteps approaching on a quiet street, his nervous system responds as if the hallway outside his childhood bedroom still exists. These triggers hit him without warning, and in the moments after, he finds himself either driving recklessly — taking corners too fast, running yellow lights, doing things he recognises are dangerous — or reaching for the small bag of marijuana he keeps in the centre console, smoking between fares to bring his heart rate down. He has also begun using harder substances on weekends. The distraction and the drugs work, in the short term, which is why he keeps returning to them.

What Kwame has come to believe about himself is perhaps more disabling than any single symptom. He is certain that he has been permanently changed — that something essential was broken in those years that cannot be repaired. The phrase he used in session was: "I'm not the same as other people my age." He has pulled away from the Ghanaian community his mother once kept him connected to, skipping the church gatherings and cultural events he attended through his twenties, convinced that the disconnection he feels is visible, that people can see what was done to him. This belief that he is fundamentally altered deepens the sense that he cannot be safe anywhere — that even when a situation is objectively calm, his body's insistence on reacting as though danger is present proves that he cannot trust reassurance from others or from his own circumstances. This appraisal of himself as permanently damaged has pushed him further into isolation, keeping intimacy at a distance and reinforcing the drug use as the only reliable management tool he has — which, over months, has stripped away more of the community and connection that might otherwise have contradicted his darkest beliefs about himself.

The hypervigilance and the avoidance now feed each other in ways Kwame is beginning to dimly recognise. The more he monitors for threat — scanning every fare, tracking footsteps on the street outside his car — the more his body stays primed, and the more primed his body stays, the more easily the triggers find him. He came to the intake session, he said, not because he believes he can be fixed, but because he is tired of being afraid of himself. What he hopes for, tentatively, is to understand why his body keeps doing this to him. What he fears most is that the answer will confirm what he already suspects: that it always will.
